transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Lindqvist, thank you for coming back in. I asked you to come in because we discovered a mistake was made during your son's vaccinations earlier today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A mistake? What do you mean by a mistake?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: While we were preparing the doses, the vaccines were drawn up for the wrong weight band. This means one of the vaccines was administered at a dose intended for an older, heavier child.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're kidding. I was literally standing there. Which one? Give me the exact medication and the dosage error.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was the pediatric dose of the combined vaccine. We used the dose for the ten to fifteen kilogram bracket instead of the under ten bracket. I am very sorry. This was our mistake.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I spent fifteen years in a rig as a paramedic. I know exactly how a dosing error happens when people are lazy with their charts. You've given my son an overdose.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is a serious error.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Serious? It's a failure of basic clinical safety! How does this even happen in a well-child clinic?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We were moving quite quickly between patients and the check was missed. I apologize.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't give a damn if you were busy. My son is a baby, not a conveyor belt. Is he going to have a reaction? Is there toxicity?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It's understandably frustrating.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Frustrating? I'm beyond frustrated, I'm furious. I trusted you with his health and you can't even get the weight band right.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know you're angry.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You have no idea. I want to know exactly what the toxicity profile is for the excess amount he received. Now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I actually have the specific plan for the next few hours ready. First, we have already contacted the toxicology pharmacy to confirm the ceiling dose for this specific agent. Second, I need you to monitor his temperature every two hours for the next twenty-four hours. If it exceeds thirty-eight degrees, you call this direct line immediately. Third, we have scheduled a follow-up blood panel for tomorrow morning at eight to check his renal function.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Why does he need blood work?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: To be absolutely certain there is no systemic impact from the higher dose. You'll bring him to the lab at eight, and I will personally review those results by ten. I will call you at ten-fifteen with the findings.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And what happens if the results are abnormal?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: If there's any deviation from the norm, we have a protocol to admit him for observation and fluid management. I've already alerted the pediatric lead and the on-call consultant so they are expecting him if that happens.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is a nightmare. I can't believe I have to spend my tomorrow morning at a lab because you couldn't read a scale.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I realize this is a huge burden on you and your family.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're just saying that.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am. And to make sure this doesn't happen to anyone else, I've already filed an incident report. Starting tomorrow, our clinic is implementing a dual-signature verification for all weight-based dosing before the needle even touches the patient.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Well, that's great for the next kid. What about my son?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That's why I'm staying on top of these tests tomorrow. I'll be the one managing his follow-up personally.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I still want the written report of the dosage error for my own records.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will print that out for you right now, including the exact milligrams administered versus the intended dose, and I'll give it to you before you leave today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Fine. I'm still not happy about this.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I completely understand. I'll get that paperwork and then I'll walk you out.

H.justification: The resident never interrupts the patient, remains regulated despite aggressive pushback, and uses no rushing language.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly in the first turn, but there were no comprehension checks performed throughout the conversation.

A.justification: The resident uses direct apology language ('I am very sorry', 'I apologize') and takes full responsibility without deflection.

R.justification: The resident names specific emotions ('frustrating', 'angry') and references the patient's specific burden regarding the lab visit.

T.justification: The resident provides specific steps (temp monitoring, blood panel), clear timelines (8am, 10am, 10:15am), the patient's role (monitoring/bringing child to lab), and a prevention plan (dual-signature verification).
